warmup.q: A MutableStateFlow<Int>(0) has one collector that takes 100 ms per value. Code sets value = 1, 2 and 3 within a millisecond, and later sets 3 again. Which values does the collector see?
options: Only 3, because the collector started late
warmup.why: A StateFlow holds one current value, like the board in the hall. A busy collector doesn't get a queue of what it missed; it gets the latest value when it's ready, so 1 and 2 are skipped. Setting a value equal to the current one does nothing at all, so the second 3 never arrives.

opening:
In the hall of a busy house hangs a board that shows today's menu. Whoever walks past glances at it and sees what's for dinner now. Nobody reads yesterday's menu off it, and if the cook changes her mind three times before lunch, the board just shows the last choice. In the kitchen there's also a bell. When dinner is ready, the cook rings it, and everyone in the house who is listening hears it at that moment. Whoever comes home later hears nothing.

The flows of Flow basics were neither. A cold flow is a recipe card: it does nothing until someone cooks from it. Some values live on their own, whether anyone looks or not, such as the status of a dish or an announcement for the whole house. The easy traps are to use the board for announcements, and to ring a bell that nobody can hear while they're busy.

In this lesson, we'll build the board and the bell, see what each one loses, let many screens share one cold flow, and keep the writable version private. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a board in the hall that always shows today's menu and a bell that everyone in the house hears when it rings. A StateFlow is the board: one current value, with missed and equal values skipped. A SharedFlow is the bell: every event to every listener, while its buffer has room. stateIn and shareIn let many screens share one cold flow.

Now search your own code for MutableSharedFlow() with no arguments, and for a tryEmit whose result nobody reads. Each is a bell that may ring unheard.

Next, we'll swap the bell for a hatch between two cooks. How does a queue between coroutines work, and how do you build a pipeline of workers with one?

sections.h: StateFlow is the board in the hall: one current value, and it skips what you missed
sections.html:
A StateFlow<T> is a flow that always has a value. You read it with .value at any moment, like glancing at the board. When you collect it, you get the current value first, then each new one. It is hot: it exists and holds its value whether or not anyone collects it, unlike the cold flows of Flow basics. That makes it the natural type for state, a value where only the latest one matters: the status of a dish, the oven's temperature, today's menu.

Java
// Java equivalent: a Reactor sink that replays its latest value, with repeats filtered out
Sinks.Many<Menu> board = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(new Menu("tomato"));
board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("onion"));
board.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(this::show);
Kotlin
val board = MutableStateFlow(Menu(soup = "tomato"))
board.value = Menu(soup = "onion")     // set from any thread
println(board.value)                    // Menu(soup=onion)
board.collect { show(it) }              // current value first, then each change; never returns

Two rules make a StateFlow cheap, and both surprise people. Updates are conflated: a slow collector doesn't get a queue of the values it missed, it gets the latest one when it's ready. And a StateFlow compares with equals. Setting a value equal to the current one does nothing, and no collector wakes up. With a data class, a new object with the same fields counts as equal.

Predict the output before you read on. StateFlowConflation, in the Try it below, has a board in the hall that takes 100 ms to chalk up each menu. The cook changes the soup three times while the first one is being chalked up, then sets the last one again:

the board in the hall shows tomato soup
the board in the hall shows onion soup
setting an equal menu again (a new object, same fields)
value is onion; the collector is still waiting, because a StateFlow never completes

Leek and pea never reached the board, and the second onion didn't either. Nobody chalks up "still onion".

Both rules follow from what StateFlow is underneath. Its KDoc, the documentation written in the library's source, describes MutableStateFlow(initial) as a shared flow (the next section's type) with replay = 1 and DROP_OLDEST. That shared flow starts out holding the initial value, and a distinctUntilChanged() step drops repeats on the way out.

So a StateFlow is for state. It's the wrong type for events, values where every single one matters, such as each step a dish goes through for the kitchen log, or "dinner's ready". Conflation would drop some of them without a trace.

One more thing to expect: collect on a StateFlow never returns. The KDoc says it plainly, "state flow never completes". Collect it in a coroutine you will cancel, or wait for one particular value with first: status.first { it == DishStatus.SERVED }.

A StateFlow keeps only the latest value. Use it for state, never for events.

The board shows what's true now. For what just happened, the house needs a bell.

code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking data class Menu(val soup: String) fun main() = runBlocking { val board = MutableStateFlow(Menu("tomato")) val hall = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { board.collect { menu -> println("the board in the hall shows ${menu.soup} soup") delay(100) // chalking up the board is slow } } // the cook changes her mind three times while the board is being chalked up board.value = Menu("leek") board.value = Menu("pea") board.value = Menu("onion") delay(150) println("setting an equal menu again (a new object, same fields)") board.value = Menu("onion") delay(150) println("value is ${board.value.soup}; the collector is still waiting, because a StateFlow never completes") hall.cancel() }

alt.title: StateFlowConflationJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of StateFlowConflation.kt with Reactor: a sink that replays its latest value, // distinctUntilChanged for the equality rule, and onBackpressureLatest so a slow subscriber only // gets the newest value. StateFlow does all three by itself. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class StateFlowConflationJava { record Menu(String soup) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Menu> board = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(new Menu("tomato")); Disposable hall = board.asFlux() .distinctUntilChanged() .onBackpressureLatest() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) // request one value at a time .subscribe(menu -> { System.out.println("the board in the hall shows " + menu.soup() + " soup"); sleep(100); // chalking up the board is slow }); Thread.sleep(20); // the cook changes her mind three times while the board is being chalked up board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("leek")); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("pea")); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("onion")); Thread.sleep(250); System.out.println("setting an equal menu again (a new object, same fields)"); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("onion")); Thread.sleep(150); hall.dispose(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: The board shows tomato soup, then onion soup: leek and pea are skipped. Setting the equal menu again prints nothing. With a plain class, equality falls back to identity, so the "equal" menu is a new value, and the board shows onion soup a second time. The Java twin prints the same two board lines, using replay().latestOrDefault, distinctUntilChanged and onBackpressureLatest.

video.title: StateFlow keeps one latest value and skips what a slow collector missed; SharedFlow's buffer and replay decide which events get through

sections.h: SharedFlow is the house bell, and its buffer decides which rings are lost
sections.html:
A MutableSharedFlow<T> is the house bell. It sends every value to every current subscriber, each coroutine collecting it at that moment. (A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without holding a thread.) It has no current value of its own. Three parameters decide what it keeps:

Java
// Java equivalent: a multicast Reactor sink with a buffer for slow subscribers
Sinks.Many<String> bell = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false);
Sinks.EmitResult result = bell.tryEmitNext("dinner's ready");   // FAIL_OVERFLOW when full
Kotlin
val bell = MutableSharedFlow<String>(
    replay = 0,                                 // late listeners get no history
    extraBufferCapacity = 64,                   // room for rings a busy listener hasn't heard yet
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND,  // when full: emit waits, tryEmit returns false
)

replay is how many recent values a new subscriber gets first. extraBufferCapacity is room beyond that for values that slow subscribers haven't taken yet. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when all of it is full. SUSPEND, the default, makes emit wait for the slowest subscriber. DROP_OLDEST throws away the oldest buffered value, and DROP_LATEST throws away the new one. The two drop policies need some replay or buffer to work with.

emit is a suspend function. tryEmit is its twin for code that can't suspend, such as a callback from an older library, and it's the impatient one: it never waits for anybody. If the value doesn't fit, it returns false and walks off.

Here's the trap, and it's easy to fall into because the defaults look harmless. With the default parameters there is no buffer at all. So tryEmit fails whenever the flow has a subscriber, even an idle one waiting for a value, and the value is lost unless you check the result. With no buffer, only the suspending emit can hand a value over, and it waits until every subscriber has taken it. With no subscriber at all, tryEmit returns true, and the value goes nowhere. The lab's starting code has exactly this bug.

SharedFlowEvents, in the Try it below, rings the bell five times with tryEmit while its one listener needs 50 ms to write each ring in the log. Predict each line:

default (no replay, no buffer)           tryEmit: [false, false, false, false, false]  received: []
extraBufferCapacity = 2                  tryEmit: [true, true, false, false, false]  received: [e1, e2]
extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST     tryEmit: [true, true, true, true, true]  received: [e4, e5]
extraBufferCapacity = 64                 tryEmit: [true, true, true, true, true]  received: [e1, e2, e3, e4, e5]
a late subscriber to replay = 2 first gets: [e4, e5]

The default bell rang five times and reached nobody. A buffer of 2 took two rings and refused the rest. DROP_OLDEST said true five times and quietly threw three rings away. Only the buffer of 64 delivered everything.

Here the bell picture breaks. A real bell rings for whoever is in the house, and a listener in the shower simply misses it. A SharedFlow with a buffer keeps each ring for a busy listener until they're ready, and when the buffer is full, SUSPEND makes the ringer wait. In an empty house, though, the two agree: a value emitted while nobody subscribes is gone, apart from the replay cache. If events must survive having no listener, you want something else: a Channel with one consumer (lesson 9 of this track), or a file or a database.

Side by side: a StateFlow has a value, replays exactly one, conflates and skips duplicates. A SharedFlow has no value, replays what you configure, and with a buffer and SUSPEND it delivers every event to every subscriber. Both are safe to emit into from many threads, the workers that run code, at once. Reactor's sinks, its objects for pushing values into a Flux, aren't by default: concurrent tryEmitNext calls can fail with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED.

A default MutableSharedFlow() has no buffer. Give it one, and check what tryEmit returns.

The board and the bell are hot from the start. Often, though, the values come from a cold flow, and you want many screens to share one run of it.

code.title: SharedFlowEvents.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Rings the bell five times with tryEmit while the one listener is busy, and reports what got through. */ suspend fun tryFive(label: String, events: MutableSharedFlow<String>) = kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope { val received = mutableListOf<String>() val listener = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { delay(50); received += it } // writing each ring in the log takes 50 ms } val accepted = (1..5).map { events.tryEmit("e$it") } delay(400) listener.cancel() println("%-40s tryEmit: %s received: %s".format(label, accepted, received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { tryFive("default (no replay, no buffer)", MutableSharedFlow()) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 64", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64)) // replay: what a subscriber that arrives later gets first val replayed = MutableSharedFlow<String>(replay = 2) (1..5).forEach { replayed.emit("e$it") } // no subscribers yet println("a late subscriber to replay = 2 first gets: ${replayed.replayCache}") }

alt.title: SharedFlowEventsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SharedFlowEvents.kt with Reactor sinks: a multicast sink with a bounded // buffer refuses values when a slow subscriber can't keep up (FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false), // and a replay sink keeps the last N values for late subscribers. Reactor sizes small buffers up // to its own minimum, so this twin sends 20 events instead of 5 to fill one. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class SharedFlowEventsJava { static void tryTwenty(String label, Sinks.Many<String> events) throws InterruptedException { List<String> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Disposable listener = events.asFlux() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) .subscribe(e -> { sleep(50); received.add(e); }); // writing each ring in the log takes 50 ms List<Sinks.EmitResult> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) results.add(events.tryEmitNext("e" + i)); Thread.sleep(1_200); listener.dispose(); long ok = results.stream().filter(r -> r == Sinks.EmitResult.OK).count(); System.out.printf("%-26s tryEmitNext OK: %2d, FAIL_OVERFLOW: %2d received %2d events%n", label, ok, results.size() - ok, received.size()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 2", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2, false)); tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 64", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false)); Sinks.Many<String> replayed = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) replayed.tryEmitNext("e" + i); // no subscribers yet List<String> late = new ArrayList<>(); replayed.asFlux().subscribe(late::add).dispose(); System.out.println("a late subscriber to replay().limit(2) first gets: " + late); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: Default: [false, false, false, false, false] and nothing received: with no buffer, tryEmit can't hand anything over while there is a subscriber, busy or not. Buffer of 2: two true, then false, and [e1, e2] received. Buffer of 2 with DROP_OLDEST: every tryEmit returns true, but only [e4, e5] arrive, because the older ones were dropped. Buffer of 64: everything gets through. The late subscriber to replay = 2 gets [e4, e5]. Adding replay = 1 changes nothing in that line, because the subscriber was there from the start. The Java twin reports FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false, and only after 9 values (it sends 20), because Reactor rounds small buffers up.

sections.h: Share one cold flow among many screens with stateIn and shareIn
sections.html:
A cold flow runs once per collector, as Flow basics showed. Picture a cold flow that reads the oven thermometer every 100 ms, and three screens around the house that show the temperature. Each screen collects the flow, so the thermometer is read three times as often as it needs to be.

stateIn and shareIn run the upstream, the cold flow they read from, just once. They run it in a scope you give them, the owner of coroutines from Structured concurrency, and share its values with every collector:

Java
// Java equivalent: one shared upstream that starts with the first subscriber
// and stops 5 seconds after the last one leaves
Flux<Integer> temperature = thermometerReadings
    .replay(1)
    .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
Kotlin
val temperature: StateFlow<Int> = thermometerReadings     // a cold flow
    .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = 0)

stateIn gives a StateFlow, so it needs an initial value. shareIn(scope, started, replay) gives a SharedFlow. The started argument decides when the shared upstream runs:

  • SharingStarted.Eagerly starts at once, before any subscriber, and runs until the scope is cancelled.
  • SharingStarted.Lazily starts with the first subscriber and then never stops.
  • SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) starts with the first subscriber and stops once the last one has been gone for stopTimeoutMillis. The default is 0. A few seconds is common, so a screen that restarts doesn't restart the upstream.

StateInDemo, in the Try it below, shares the thermometer with WhileSubscribed(300). Two screens subscribe at 200 ms and leave 250 ms later. Predict when reading starts and stops:

   79 ms  stateIn returned; waiting 200 ms before the first screen
  327 ms  two screens subscribed
  344 ms  thermometer: reading started
  581 ms  both screens left; temperature.value = 182
  884 ms  thermometer: reading stopped
 1081 ms  done

Reading started once, for both screens, and stopped about 300 ms after they left. Run with -Pargs=eagerly, the same demo started reading at 62 ms, before anyone was watching.

The scope owns the shared collection, so make it a long-lived scope you control, like the Oven's scope in Structured concurrency. A scope that belongs to one short call would end the sharing when the call ends, and GlobalScope would never end it. In tests, the test library's backgroundScope plays that part.

Sharing doesn't make the upstream any less cold. When WhileSubscribed stops it and a new subscriber arrives later, the upstream runs again from the top. The readings restart, and a running total built with runningFold, the operator that keeps a running total, starts again from its initial value. For a live display that's what you want. For a total that must survive restarts, keep it somewhere durable and use the flow only to show it.

stateIn and shareIn run one cold flow for many collectors. Give them a scope you own.

Now we can build a class that owns some state and shares it. One question is left: who is allowed to change it?

code.title: StateInDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SharingStarted import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onCompletion import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onStart import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.stateIn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var t0 = 0L private fun at(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { t0 = System.nanoTime() val started = when (args.firstOrNull()) { "eagerly" -> SharingStarted.Eagerly "lazily" -> SharingStarted.Lazily else -> SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 300) } // a cold flow that reads the oven thermometer every 100 ms val readings = flow { var n = 0 while (true) { emit(180 + n++); delay(100) } }.onStart { at("thermometer: reading started") }.onCompletion { at("thermometer: reading stopped") } val appScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) // the owner of the sharing val temperature = readings.stateIn(appScope, started, initialValue = 0) at("stateIn returned; waiting 200 ms before the first screen") delay(200) val hall = launch { temperature.collect { } } val kitchen = launch { temperature.collect { } } at("two screens subscribed") delay(250) hall.cancel(); kitchen.cancel() at("both screens left; temperature.value = ${temperature.value}") delay(500) at("done") appScope.cancel() }

alt.title: StateInDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of StateInDemo.kt with Reactor: replay(1).refCount(1, grace) shares one // upstream between subscribers, starts it with the first one, and stops it when the last one // has been gone for the grace period, like stateIn with WhileSubscribed(300). package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.time.Duration; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class StateInDemoJava { static long t0; static void at(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { t0 = System.nanoTime(); // a cold flux that reads the oven thermometer every 100 ms Flux<Long> readings = Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofMillis(100)) .map(n -> 180 + n) .doOnSubscribe(s -> at("thermometer: reading started")) .doOnCancel(() -> at("thermometer: reading stopped")); Flux<Long> temperature = readings.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofMillis(300)); at("refCount returned; waiting 200 ms before the first screen"); Thread.sleep(200); Disposable hall = temperature.subscribe(); Disposable kitchen = temperature.subscribe(); at("two screens subscribed"); Thread.sleep(250); hall.dispose(); kitchen.dispose(); at("both screens left"); Thread.sleep(500); at("done"); } }

try.expect: With WhileSubscribed(300), reading starts only when the screens subscribe, at about 200 ms, once for both, and stops about 300 ms after they leave. With eagerly, reading starts at once, before anyone subscribes, and stops only when the scope is cancelled at the end. With lazily, it starts with the first screen and never stops on its own (the line after done is the scope being cancelled). The Java twin starts and stops at the same moments as the WhileSubscribed run.

sections.h: Keep the writable flow private, and change it in one step
sections.html:
A class that owns some state should let callers read it, and nobody else write it. Picture a tracker for one dish: the board in the hall shows its status (waiting, cooking, served), and only the kitchen may move it on. Before Kotlin 2.4, that took two properties:

Java
// Java equivalent: a private sink and a public read-only view
class DishTracker {
    private final Sinks.Many<DishStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(DishStatus.WAITING);

    public Flux<DishStatus> status() { return status.asFlux(); }

    void startCooking() { status.tryEmitNext(DishStatus.COOKING); }
}
Kotlin
class DishTracker {
    private val _status = MutableStateFlow(DishStatus.WAITING)
    val status: StateFlow<DishStatus> = _status.asStateFlow()

    fun startCooking() { _status.value = DishStatus.COOKING }
}

A property's backing field is the hidden storage behind it. Kotlin 2.4.0 made explicit backing fields stable: a property can declare its field, with a more specific type than the property itself. They arrived as experimental in 2.3.0, whose release notes used exactly this case as their example:

class DishTracker {
    val status: StateFlow<DishStatus>
        field = MutableStateFlow(DishStatus.WAITING)

    fun startCooking() { status.value = DishStatus.COOKING }   // smart-cast inside the class
}

Outside the class, status is a StateFlow with no setter. Inside it, the compiler knows the field is a MutableStateFlow and smart-casts, that is, treats it as the more specific type without a cast. One small difference remains. asStateFlow() returns a wrapper, so a caller can't cast it back to MutableStateFlow. An explicit backing field hides the type only at compile time. Both are fine in application code. In a library other people build on, the wrapper is the stricter choice.

Then write every change as one atomic step. count.value = count.value + 1 is a read-modify-write, the race from Race conditions in the first track: two threads both read 41, both write 42, and one plate goes uncounted. StateUpdates, in the Try it below, lets 8 helpers each count 100,000 plates:

value = value + 1                  expected 800000, got 457636
update { it + 1 }                  expected 800000, got 800000

Over 340,000 plates were served and never counted. count.update { it + 1 } retries with compare-and-set, an atomic "change it only if nobody beat me to it", until it wins. status.compareAndSet(expected, new) moves only if the value is still expected, and returns whether it did. That's how the lab's tracker makes sure two helpers can't both serve the same dish: the loser's compareAndSet fails, it reads the new status, and the move is no longer allowed.

The same habit applies to the bell. Ring it from the method that changes the state, after the change has succeeded, so the kitchen log never describes a move that didn't happen.

Expose the read-only type, keep the writable one inside, and change it with update or compareAndSet.

try.title: Lose plates with value = value + 1
steps: Read StateUpdates.kt. Eight coroutines on Default each add a plate 100,000 times. Predict both totals.
Run it twice.
Run the Java twin, which does the same with an AtomicReference.

code.title: StateUpdates.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** 8 helpers on Default each add 1 plate to a shared count 100,000 times. */ suspend fun countPlates(label: String, add: (MutableStateFlow<Long>) -> Unit) { val platesServed = MutableStateFlow(0L) coroutineScope { repeat(8) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(100_000) { add(platesServed) } } } } println("%-34s expected 800000, got %d".format(label, platesServed.value)) } fun main() = runBlocking { countPlates("value = value + 1") { it.value = it.value + 1 } // read-modify-write: loses updates countPlates("update { it + 1 }") { it.update { plates -> plates + 1 } } // compare-and-set in a loop }

alt.title: StateUpdatesJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of StateUpdates.kt: the same read-modify-write race on an AtomicReference, // fixed the same way, with a compare-and-set loop (updateAndGet). package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateUpdatesJava { /** 8 helpers each add 1 plate to a shared count 100,000 times. */ static void countPlates(String label, Consumer<AtomicReference<Long>> add) { AtomicReference<Long> platesServed = new AtomicReference<>(0L); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) add.accept(platesServed); }); } System.out.printf("%-34s expected 800000, got %d%n", label, platesServed.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { countPlates("set(get() + 1)", ref -> ref.set(ref.get() + 1)); // read-modify-write: loses updates countPlates("updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)", ref -> ref.updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)); // compare-and-set in a loop } }

try.expect: value = value + 1 comes out far short of 800,000, and the number changes from run to run (457,636 in one run here). update { it + 1 } gives exactly 800,000 every time. The Java twin loses updates with set(get() + 1) (303,507 here) and gets 800,000 with updateAndGet, because it's the same race and the same fix.

refs.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.4.0 (explicit backing fields)

compare.title: A dish tracker: Reactor sinks vs StateFlow and SharedFlow

java.title: DishTracker.java
java.html: class DishTracker { private final AtomicReference<DishStatus> current = new AtomicReference<>(DishStatus.WAITING); private final Sinks.Many<DishStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(DishStatus.WAITING); private final Sinks.Many<Transition> transitions = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); public DishStatus currentStatus() { return current.get(); } // 1. a synchronous read public Flux<DishStatus> status() { return status.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged(); } public Flux<Transition> transitions() { return transitions.asFlux(); } boolean moveTo(DishStatus next) { DishStatus from = current.get(); if (!from.canMoveTo(next) || !current.compareAndSet(from, next)) return false; // 2. atomic move // 3. sinks reject concurrent emits (FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED), so serialize them synchronized (this) { status.tryEmitNext(next); transitions.tryEmitNext(new Transition(dish, from, next)); } return true; } }

kotlin.title: DishTracker.kt
kotlin.html: class DishTracker(private val dish: String) { val status: StateFlow<DishStatus> // 1. .value is a synchronous read field = MutableStateFlow(DishStatus.WAITING) val transitions: SharedFlow<Transition> field = MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64) fun moveTo(next: DishStatus): Boolean { while (true) { val from = status.value if (!from.canMoveTo(next)) return false if (status.compareAndSet(from, next)) { // 2. atomic move check(transitions.tryEmit(Transition(dish, from, next))) // 3. safe from any thread return true } } } }

compare.note: The Kotlin version needs fewer moving parts, because a StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it synchronously, compareAndSet changes it atomically, and collectors see changes with conflation and de-duplication built in. Reactor has no single type for that, so the Java version keeps an AtomicReference for the value and a replaying sink for the stream, and must keep the two in step. The other real difference is concurrency. MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow are documented as safe for emitters on many threads. Reactor's default sinks detect concurrent tryEmitNext calls and fail them with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED, so the Java tracker serializes its emits with a lock.

worked.title: Share one oven reading among every phone in the house

steps.say: A family app shows the oven's temperature on every phone in the house. Each open phone collects temperatures(), a cold flow that asks the smart oven every second. With six phones open, the oven's small web server gets six questions a second and starts refusing some of them.
steps.code: fun temperatures(): Flow<Int> = flow { while (true) { emit(oven.readCelsius()) // one call to the oven per collector per second delay(1.seconds) } } // on each phone's screen temperatures().collect { show(it) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same design: a cold Flux subscribed once per phone Flux<Integer> temperatures() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> oven.readCelsius()); // one call per subscriber per second } // on each phone's screen temperatures().subscribe(this::show);

steps.say: Decide the type first. A phone wants the latest temperature, and a phone that missed a reading doesn't need it replayed, so this is state: a StateFlow.
Share the upstream in a scope that lives as long as the app, and stop it when nobody watches. Five seconds of grace covers a phone that locks its screen for a moment.
steps.code: class OvenFeed(oven: SmartOven) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) // 1. the owner of the sharing val celsius: StateFlow<Int?> = flow { while (true) { emit(oven.readCelsius()); delay(1.seconds) } }.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = null) // 2. one call for all override fun close() = scope.cancel() // 3. ends with the app }

alt.html: class OvenFeed { // 1. and 2.: one shared upstream, started by the first subscriber, stopped 5 s after the last final Flux<Integer> celsius; OvenFeed(SmartOven oven) { this.celsius = Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> oven.readCelsius()) .replay(1) .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } }

steps.say: Each phone now collects the shared StateFlow. A slow phone gets the newest reading rather than a backlog, and a reading equal to the last one isn't sent again at all.
steps.code: // on each phone's screen: no extra call to the oven ovenFeed.celsius.filterNotNull().collect { show(it) }

alt.html: // on each phone's screen: no extra call to the oven ovenFeed.celsius.distinctUntilChanged().onBackpressureLatest().subscribe(this::show);

steps.say: Self-check: why not SharingStarted.Eagerly? (It would ask the oven every second from the moment the app starts, even at night with every phone asleep, and never stop until the app closes. WhileSubscribed asks only while someone is watching.)

lab.title: A dish tracker and a live plate count
steps: Meet the code. DishStatus.kt lists the statuses a dish moves through and the moves allowed between them. DishTracker tracks one dish: helpers call moveTo from their own threads, the board reads status, and the kitchen log collects transitions. It already uses explicit backing fields, so status is read-only outside the class. liveServedCount shares a running count of plates served. Run the tests: five of seven fail.
Give transitions a buffer: MutableSharedFlow(replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 64). The two transition tests should pass.

Make moveTo atomic: in a loop, read status.value, check canMoveTo, call beforeMove, then status.compareAndSet(from, next). If the compare-and-set fails, go round again. Emit the transition only after it succeeds.
In LiveCount.kt, replace SharingStarted.Eagerly with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000).
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Inside the class, status smart-casts to MutableStateFlow, so status.compareAndSet(from, next) and transitions.tryEmit(...) compile without a cast.
Check what tryEmit returns. With a buffer of 64 it should always be true here; check(...) turns a surprise false into a loud failure instead of a lost transition.
The race test holds both helpers in beforeMove until both have read COOKING. With compareAndSet, the second one's move fails, it reads SERVED, and canMoveTo says no.
The stateIn tests run on virtual time, the test library's pretend clock, so WhileSubscribed(5_000) takes no real time at all.

drill.title: A smoke alarm's state, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class SmokeAlarm with a read-only state: StateFlow<AlarmState> (QUIET at first) backed by a writable one, fun trip(): Boolean that moves QUIET to RINGING atomically and returns whether this call did it, and events: SharedFlow<String> that code which can't suspend can publish to with tryEmit, even while a subscriber is busy.

answer.html: class SmokeAlarm { val state: StateFlow<AlarmState> field = MutableStateFlow(AlarmState.QUIET) val events: SharedFlow<String> field = MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64) fun trip(): Boolean { if (!state.compareAndSet(AlarmState.QUIET, AlarmState.RINGING)) return false check(events.tryEmit("alarm ringing")) return true } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: an atomic holder for the state, a buffered multicast sink for events class SmokeAlarm { private final AtomicReference<AlarmState> state = new AtomicReference<>(AlarmState.QUIET); private final Sinks.Many<String> events = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); AlarmState state() { return state.get(); } Flux<String> events() { return events.asFlux(); } synchronized boolean trip() { // synchronized: Reactor sinks reject concurrent emits if (!state.compareAndSet(AlarmState.QUIET, AlarmState.RINGING)) return false; events.tryEmitNext("alarm ringing").orThrow(); return true; } }

recap: A StateFlow is hot and always has a value. It conflates (slow collectors get only the latest) and skips values equal to the current one, so it's for state, not events.
A SharedFlow sends every value to every subscriber. replay is history for late subscribers, extraBufferCapacity is room for slow ones, and onBufferOverflow says what happens when both are full.
With default parameters a MutableSharedFlow has no buffer, so tryEmit fails whenever the flow has a subscriber, even an idle one. Give it a buffer and check the result.
stateIn and shareIn run a cold upstream once in a scope you own and share it. WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) starts with the first subscriber and stops after the last one has left.
Expose state read-only with an explicit backing field (stable since Kotlin 2.4) or asStateFlow(), and change it with update { } or compareAndSet, never value = value + 1.
The limit: both hot flows live in memory. A value emitted while nobody subscribes is gone, apart from the replay cache, and nothing survives a restart.

explain.prompt: A friend stores each step a dish goes through in a MutableStateFlow<Transition?> so the kitchen log can collect them, and the log is missing entries on busy evenings. Explain why, and what you would use instead.
explain.answer: A StateFlow holds one current value, so it's built to drop history. When the log is busy writing one transition and two more happen, it only gets the latest one when it's ready, and the middle one is gone. It also skips a value equal to the current one, so a repeated transition never arrives. That's right for state like "the current status", but transitions are events, and every one matters. I'd use a MutableSharedFlow with no replay and an extraBufferCapacity big enough for a busy evening, keep the default SUSPEND overflow, and check what tryEmit returns, so a full buffer shows up as an error instead of a missing line. And because it all lives in memory, anything that must survive a restart should also be written somewhere durable, such as a file or a database.

deeper.html:
MutableSharedFlow has a subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>. It is deliberately not conflated, so you can react to the first subscriber arriving or the last one leaving, for example to open and close a connection to a slow device. SharingStarted is an interface, and WhileSubscribed is written on top of exactly that count. A custom strategy can start sharing only at certain hours, or only after a warm-up.

WhileSubscribed has a second parameter, replayExpirationMillis, which defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE. It decides how long the last value stays in the replay cache after the upstream stops. Set it to 0 if a stale value is worse than none, for instance an oven temperature that must never be shown once the oven has been switched off.

stateIn and shareIn keep a coroutine running in the scope you give them, so the scope's life is the sharing's life. If the upstream throws, that coroutine fails, the error goes up into the scope, and the StateFlow simply stops updating. Put a catch or retryWhen on the upstream, above stateIn, and decide what the subscribers should see while it recovers.

kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 added two small helpers. SharedFlow.asFlow() returns a view that hides the hot-flow type, so callers can't rely on it being shared. And there is now an onSubscription overload on StateFlow that keeps the StateFlow type. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, marked experimental. For plain counters shared between coroutines they are an alternative to a StateFlow that nobody collects, which lesson 10 of this track compares with Mutex.

This lesson is the first look at hot flows. Hot flows in depth, in the Kotlin Flow in depth track, opens up the SharedFlow buffer slot by slot, and shows how stateIn and shareIn decide when to start and stop.
